title: Cross validation
story:
One held-out portion gives you one number from one arbitrary partition. Change which rows were set aside and the number changes, and nothing in the procedure tells you by how much. On a small dataset that variation can be larger than the differences you are trying to detect, which means the comparison you are making is between noise and noise.

Rotating the held-out portion fixes that. Divide the data into folds, and for each fold in turn, fit on the rest and score on it. Every row is used for testing exactly once and for training every other time. Average the scores for an estimate, and look at their spread for how much that estimate would have moved under a different partition — the second of those is as useful as the first and is usually not reported.

Stone gave the general treatment in 1974, applying a generalised cross-validation criterion to both the choice and the assessment of prediction. That the paper names two uses is the thing to carry: choosing among candidates and assessing the chosen one are different jobs, and using the same folds for both reintroduces the selection problem from the previous lesson at one remove. Cross-validate to select, and you have selected on those folds; the honest estimate needs either a held-out portion never used in the selection, or an outer loop wrapped around the whole selection procedure.

On the practical parameter, Kohavi ran the experiment: over half a million runs on real-world datasets, varying the number of folds and whether folds were stratified, and concluding that the best method for model selection is ten-fold stratified cross-validation, even when computation power allows using more folds. Note the shape of that finding — more folds is not simply better, so the usual assumption that the exhaustive version must be the gold standard is wrong on its own terms.

The reason is a trade with two sides. More folds means each model trains on more data, so each estimate is less pessimistic about a model fitted on everything. But the training sets across folds overlap more, so the estimates become more correlated with each other, and averaging correlated estimates reduces variance less than averaging independent ones. At the extreme, leaving out one observation at a time, the training sets are nearly identical, the estimates are almost perfectly correlated, and you have paid for as many fits as you have rows to get an average that is barely more stable than a few folds would have given.

Two constraints carry over from the lesson on honest splitting and are not optional here. Folds must respect groups where rows repeat an entity, and must respect time where predictions run forward. And every step that learns from data is refitted inside each fold, never before the loop.

problem.name: Rotating held-out estimation
problem.shape: A single held-out portion produces one estimate from one arbitrary partition, with no indication of how much it would move under a different one.
tell: the dataset is small enough that one split feels arbitrary
two models are being compared on differences smaller than the noise
a single held-out score is quoted with no spread
folds were cut without regard to groups or time
problem.move: Rotate the held-out portion through the data, refitting every learned step inside each fold, and report the spread of the fold scores as well as their mean. Stratify the folds, respect groups and time order when the data has them, and wrap the whole selection procedure in an outer loop when you need an estimate of the model you chose.
problem.invariant: Each row is scored exactly once by a model that never saw it, and the average estimates the performance of the fitting procedure rather than of any single fitted model.
problem.breaks: The fold estimates are not independent, because their training sets overlap, and the overlap grows with the number of folds. So the spread across folds understates the true uncertainty, and increasing folds toward the exhaustive limit buys progressively less stability for linearly more computation.

cost.time: one fit per fold, multiplied again by every candidate when used for selection, which is where the cost becomes serious
cost.space: none beyond holding the fold assignment
cost.beats: a single split, which gives an estimate with no measure of its own variability, and the exhaustive version, which costs a fit per row for correlated estimates that barely stabilise the average

worked.problem: Why ten folds rather than as many folds as there are rows?
worked.reasoning:
Because the estimates from different folds are not independent, and that correlation grows as the folds get smaller, so the exhaustive version costs the most and buys the least.

Take the trade apart. Increasing the number of folds makes each training set larger and closer to the full dataset, which reduces the pessimism of the estimate — a model trained on ninety percent of the data is a better stand-in for one trained on everything than a model trained on half. That is the argument in favour, and it is real.

Against it: as the folds get smaller the training sets overlap more and more. At the exhaustive extreme, two training sets differ by exactly two observations, so the fitted models are nearly identical and their scores are almost perfectly correlated. Averaging correlated estimates reduces variance far less than averaging independent ones, so the average barely stabilises while the computation grows linearly in the number of rows.

You are therefore paying for one fit per observation to obtain an average that a much smaller number of folds would have given you nearly as well. The empirical answer is the one from the large study — over half a million runs across real datasets, varying folds and stratification, concluding that ten-fold stratified cross-validation is the best method for model selection even when computation allows using more folds. The phrase even when computation allows is the part that matters: this is not a compromise for the sake of speed, it is the better estimator.

Stratification is the other half of that recommendation and deserves its own line. Cutting folds at random lets the class proportions drift between them, especially when a class is small, so some folds carry a different problem from others and the variance across folds reflects the partition rather than the model. Stratifying holds the proportions fixed and removes that source of noise.

Two things I would add unprompted. The spread across folds is not a confidence interval — the estimates are correlated, so it understates the true uncertainty and should be read as an indication rather than a measurement. And folds must respect the structure of the data: grouped rows go into the same fold, and folds run forward in time where predictions do, or the whole procedure inherits exactly the leakage it was meant to protect against.

problem.practice: Score a model with five, ten and leave-one-out cross-validation on the same data, and record both the mean and the wall-clock time for each. Then run ten-fold twice with different random fold assignments and see how much the mean moves between them — that movement is what a single split was hiding.

beats.broke: A single held-out portion gives one estimate from one arbitrary partition, so the number depends on which rows happened to be set aside and carries no indication of how much it would have moved under a different draw.
beats.fix: Rotate the held-out portion through the data, fitting and scoring once per fold, so every row is used for testing exactly once and for training every other time — and read the spread of the fold scores as well as their average.
beats.cost: The model is fitted once per fold, the estimates share training data and so are not independent, and what is estimated is the performance of a recipe rather than of any single fitted model.

interview.q: Why ten folds rather than as many folds as there are rows?
interview.trap: Answering that the exhaustive version is the gold standard and ten folds is the affordable approximation. The large empirical study recommends ten-fold stratified even when computation allows more — because overlapping training sets make the estimates correlated, so more folds buy progressively less stability.
interview.answer:
Because the fold estimates are not independent, and the correlation grows as folds shrink — so the exhaustive version costs the most and buys the least.

The trade has two sides. More folds means each training set is larger and closer to the full dataset, which makes the estimate less pessimistic: a model trained on ninety percent of the data stands in better for one trained on everything than a model trained on half. That argument is real.

Against it, smaller folds mean the training sets overlap more. At the exhaustive extreme two training sets differ by exactly two observations, so the fitted models are nearly identical and their scores almost perfectly correlated. Averaging correlated estimates reduces variance far less than averaging independent ones, so the average barely stabilises while computation grows linearly in the number of rows. You pay one fit per observation for something far fewer folds would have given you.

The empirical answer comes from a study of over half a million runs varying folds and stratification, which concluded that ten-fold stratified cross-validation is best for model selection even when computation allows more folds. That phrase matters: it is not a concession to speed, it is the better estimator.

Stratification is the other half. Random folds let class proportions drift, especially when a class is small, so some folds carry a different problem and the variance across folds reflects the partition rather than the model.

Two additions. The spread across folds is not a confidence interval — the estimates are correlated, so it understates the uncertainty. And the folds must respect the data's structure: grouped rows together, folds running forward in time where predictions do, or the procedure inherits the leakage it was meant to prevent.

takeaway: Rotating the held-out portion turns one arbitrary number into an average plus a spread — but the folds share training data, so their estimates are correlated, which is why ten folds beats one per row even when you can afford the latter.
